content: Levonorgestrel is a medication used by women to prevent pregnancy after unprotected sexual intercourse or failure of a primary birth control method, such as a broken condom. However, its effectiveness may be reduced in women who weigh more than 164 pounds (74 kilograms) or those who have taken certain medications within the past month. This reduced efficacy can increase the risk of pregnancy. It is important to check the product label for ingredients, as manufacturers may change formulations, and products with similar names may contain different ingredients intended for other purposes. If you are using an over-the-counter product for self-treatment, carefully read all instructions on the packaging before taking the medication. If you have any questions, consult your pharmacist. Take one tablet orally, with or without food, as soon as possible after unprotected intercourse. After taking this medication, the timing and flow of your menstrual period may change. Notify your doctor immediately if your period is more than seven days late. Common side effects of levonorgestrel include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fatigue, dizziness, changes in vaginal bleeding, breast tenderness, and headaches. If your doctor has prescribed this medication, they have determined that the benefits outweigh the risks of side effects. Serious allergic reactions to this drug are rare. If you experience any unusual or severe symptoms, contact your doctor for medical advice. This is not a comprehensive list of side effects. Before taking levonorgestrel, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it, other progestins (e.g., norethindrone), or any other substances. This product may contain inactive ingredients that could cause allergic reactions or other issues. Levonorgestrel may cause dizziness, and consuming alcohol or marijuana can worsen this effect. Avoid driving, operating machinery, or performing tasks requiring alertness until you can do so safely. Limit alcoholic beverages. This medication should not be used during pregnancy. While it passes into breast milk, it is unlikely to harm a nursing infant. Drug interactions may alter how levonorgestrel works or increase the risk of serious side effects. Some medications, such as rifamycins (e.g., rifampin, rifabutin), St. John’s wort, seizure medications (e.g., barbiturates, carbamazepine, phenytoin, primidone, topiramate), and certain HIV drugs (e.g., nelfinavir, nevirapine), may reduce the effectiveness of levonorgestrel by decreasing the levels of birth control hormones in the body. This can result in pregnancy. Always keep a list of all medications and supplements you use and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. Overdose with this medication is unlikely. However, if someone has overdosed and exhibits severe symptoms such as loss of consciousness or difficulty breathing, call emergency services immediately. In the U.S., contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. In Canada, call 1-844-764-7669. Store levonorgestrel at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed. For further guidance, consult your pharmacist or local waste disposal company. This information is a summary and does not include all possible details about this product. It does not guarantee that the product is safe, effective, or appropriate for you. Always consult your healthcare professional for complete information about this medication and your specific health needs.
